nameStory: Sheep's sorrel gets its name because sheep and other livestock love to munch on its tangy, sour leaves. The word 'sorrel' comes from an old Germanic word meaning 'sour,' which you'll understand immediately if you taste a leaf. It's also called 'sour weed' for the same lemony, acidic flavor that makes your mouth pucker.
description: Sheep's sorrel is a low-growing perennial weed with distinctive arrow-shaped leaves that have backward-pointing lobes at their base. The plant typically grows 6-18 inches tall with reddish, deeply grooved stems that emerge from spreading underground rhizomes. In summer, it sends up tall flower spikes topped with clusters of tiny reddish or maroon flowers that give fields a rusty hue. This European native has become a common sight across New England's disturbed soils and open areas.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Arrow-shaped leaves with two backward-pointing lobes at the base, like a spearhead. The leaves feel smooth and have a distinctly sour, lemony taste when chewed. They're typically 1-4 inches long and arranged alternately up the reddish stem.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low clumps that spread by underground rhizomes, often creating patches in poor soils. The main plant stays close to the ground while flower stalks shoot up much taller in summer.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny flowers clustered on tall, upright spikes that rise well above the leaves. Female flowers are maroon or rust-colored, while male flowers are yellowish. The flower spikes give the plant a feathery appearance from a distance.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Reddish stems with deep vertical ridges that you can feel when you run your finger along them. The stems often have a wine-red or burgundy tint, especially at the base.

habitat: Thrives in poor, acidic, sandy soils where other plants struggle - think abandoned lots, roadsides, overgrazed pastures, and construction sites. You'll often find it in sunny, disturbed areas with thin, nutrient-poor soil. It's particularly common in areas with low pH where grass has trouble growing.

seasonality.spring: New arrow-shaped leaves emerge from the ground in early spring, often with a reddish tint. The sour taste is most pronounced in young spring leaves.
seasonality.summer: Tall flower spikes appear, rising 1-3 feet above the low leaf clusters. The rusty-red flower heads are most visible from June through August.
seasonality.fall: Leaves may turn reddish-brown and flower spikes dry to a rusty brown color. Seeds are dispersed and new growth may appear from spreading rhizomes.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to ground level, but the extensive rhizome system survives underground, ready to sprout new growth in spring.

funFact: Sheep's sorrel is actually edible and was historically used by sailors to prevent scurvy due to its high vitamin C content - the same sour taste that makes you pucker comes from the ascorbic acid that kept sailors healthy on long voyages!
confusionNotes: The arrow-shaped leaves might be confused with other plants, but the sour taste is unmistakable - take a tiny nibble and you'll know immediately. Wood sorrel has similar sour leaves but has heart-shaped leaflets in groups of three, not arrow shapes.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being considered a weed by many gardeners, sheep's sorrel is actually an indicator of acidic soil conditions. If you have lots of sheep's sorrel in your yard, it's telling you your soil pH is probably below 6.0.
compareHints: Unlike its larger cousins the docks (broad-leaved dock, curled dock), sheep's sorrel stays much smaller and has those distinctive backward-pointing lobes on its leaves. Common sorrel (Rumex acetosa) is similar but much larger overall with bigger, less deeply-lobed leaves. The other docks have oval or lance-shaped leaves without the arrow shape that makes sheep's sorrel so distinctive.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's dock species, broad-leaved dock is distinguished by its wide, flat-edged leaves – curled dock has wavy leaf margins, sheep's sorrel has arrow-shaped leaves, and swamp dock prefers wetland areas.
Among New England's dock species, curled dock is the easiest to identify thanks to its signature wavy leaf margins – no other dock has this feature.

Swamp dock differs from its dock relatives by its strong preference for wet habitats - while curled dock and broad-leaved dock are common weeds of dry disturbed soils, swamp dock sticks to marshes and wet areas.
Wood dock stands out dramatically from its dock relatives because of its red-veined leaves - no other dock species in New England has this feature.
Greater Water Dock stands apart from other New England docks by its wetland habitat and impressive size - it's notably larger than Curled Dock or Broad-leaved Dock.

Among the dock and sorrel family, common sorrel stands out with its distinctly arrow-shaped leaves and sour taste, while true docks like curled dock and broad-leaved dock have much larger, broader leaves without the pointed basal lobes and lack the sour flavor.
Northern dock stands out from other Rumex species by its long, narrow leaves with smooth edges - most other docks have broader leaves or wavy margins like curled dock.
Unlike its inland relatives like curled dock or broad-leaved dock, seabeach dock has much thicker, fleshier leaves and stays much lower to the ground.

Pacific golden dock stands out from other New England dock species primarily by its bright golden-yellow flowers - most relatives like curled dock and broad-leaved dock have greenish or reddish blooms.
White willow dock stands out from its dock relatives by having much narrower leaves - compare this to broad-leaved dock or curled dock which have wide, often wavy-edged leaves.
Among its dock relatives in New England, willow dock stands out with its narrow leaves - most other docks like broad-leaved dock and curled dock have much wider foliage.

Golden dock differs from other New England docks by its much smaller stature and distinctive golden flower clusters - most other docks like curled dock or broad-leaved dock are much larger perennial plants with reddish-brown flower clusters.
Golden dock stands out from its dock relatives by having much narrower leaves - more like a willow than the typical broad, paddle-shaped dock leaf.
Patience dock stands out from other New England docks by its exceptionally large size and smooth-edged leaves with heart-shaped bases.
